raw_text:
The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity in which contrast opacification of the distal epicardial coronary arteries is delayed despite absent or non-obstructive stenosis. It was first described by Tambe and colleagues in 1972 [1]. Quantification became more reproducible after the corrected thrombolysis in myocardial infarction frame count (cTFC) was introduced; a cTFC above approximately 27 frames is commonly used to define slow flow, although thresholds vary with acquisition frame rate and laboratory practice [2]. Early clinical series established that CSFP is not merely an angiographic curiosity: patients often present with rest angina or acute coronary syndrome-like symptoms, and recurrent chest pain is common [3]. Histopathological and hemodynamic studies support a microvascular substrate, including small-vessel wall thickening, luminal narrowing, increased resting microvascular tone, and impaired myocardial metabolic responses [4,5].

Reported prevalence varies by population and definition. In a contemporary catheterization cohort, Hawkins et al. found CSFP in 5.5% of patients referred for angiography, with male sex and higher body mass index independently associated with the finding [6]. Among patients with angiographically normal coronary arteries, Arbel et al. observed that slow flow frequently involved all three vessels, suggesting a diffuse rather than focal disorder [7]. Reviews have therefore framed CSFP as a distinct clinical syndrome at the interface of ischemia with non-obstructive coronary arteries and coronary microvascular dysfunction, but with a phenotype enriched for young or middle-aged men, smoking, obesity, dyslipidemia, and metabolic risk factors [8-10].

Diagnosis remains angiographic but should be cautious. Secondary causes of slow opacification—catheter damping, hypotension, left ventricular dysfunction, coronary ectasia, spasm, embolism, no-reflow after percutaneous coronary intervention, myocardial bridging, or severe valvular disease—should be excluded. Objective cTFC is preferred to visual assessment, because visual impressions can be unreliable. Recent invasive physiology data are particularly important: visual slow flow was not consistently associated with wire-based abnormalities of coronary flow reserve or microvascular resistance, emphasizing that CSFP and coronary microvascular dysfunction overlap but are not synonymous [11].

The pathobiology is heterogeneous. Endothelial dysfunction is among the most reproducible findings: brachial flow-mediated dilation is impaired in CSFP [12], and abnormal endothelin-1/nitric oxide balance at rest or during exercise suggests disordered vasomotor regulation [13-15]. Genetic and biochemical studies implicate nitric oxide synthase pathways and impaired microvascular relaxation [16]. Hyperhomocysteinemia, increased carotid intima-media thickness, and adverse long-term angina recurrence link CSFP with systemic vascular dysfunction and early atherosclerosis [17,18]. Intravascular ultrasound and fractional flow reserve studies further suggest that some patients have diffuse, angiographically “hidden” epicardial atherosclerosis contributing to resistance [19]. Thus, CSFP is best conceptualized as a final common angiographic pattern arising from variable combinations of microvascular spasm, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, platelet activation, diffuse atherosclerosis, and autonomic influences.

Clinically, patients most often report recurrent angina, frequently at rest, and may undergo repeated emergency evaluations. Objective ischemia has been demonstrated in some cohorts, but symptoms and cTFC do not always track with conventional stress testing. Electrical instability has also been reported. Increased QT dispersion in slow flow may indicate heterogeneous ventricular repolarization [26], and case reports document ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, although absolute risk remains uncertain [27]. These observations argue against dismissing CSFP as benign, while also highlighting the need for prospective outcome studies.

No therapy has been validated in large multicenter trials. Management begins with reassurance, exclusion of alternative diagnoses, and aggressive treatment of cardiovascular risk factors. Small studies suggest benefit from agents targeting endothelial dysfunction or microvascular tone. Atorvastatin improved cTFC and endothelial/inflammatory markers [20], and nicorandil improved myocardial function while modulating nitric oxide and endothelin-1 [21]. Calcium-channel strategies are biologically plausible: mibefradil improved angiographic flow and symptoms [22], and intracoronary nicardipine acutely reversed spontaneous CSFP in many vessels [23]. Dipyridamole has been associated with improved ventricular function and angiographic flow in selected patients [24,25]. Evidence for beta-blockers, nitrates, ranolazine, angiotensin-pathway drugs, and other antianginals remains limited and individualized.

Several circulating biomarkers—mean platelet volume, eosinophil count, inflammatory indices, homocysteine, and endothelial mediators—have been associated with CSFP, but none is sufficiently validated for diagnosis or risk stratification [28,29]. Overall, CSFP should be recognized as a clinically relevant, mechanistically diverse coronary vasomotor disorder. Future work should standardize angiographic definitions, incorporate invasive and non-invasive microvascular phenotyping, and test mechanism-guided therapies in adequately powered randomized trials [30].
